subject: Physics
subtopic: Simple Harmonic Motion and General Waves
stem: Which one among the following statements is not correct?
optA: In progressive waves, the amplitude may be constant and neighboring points are out of phase with each other.
optB: In air or other gases, a progressive antinode occurs at a displacement node and a progressive node occurs at a displacement antinode.
optC: Transverse wave can be polarized while longitudinal wave can not be polarized.
optD: Longitudinal wave can be polarized while transverse wave can not be polarized.
solution: Read the question carefully: it asks which statement is NOT correct. Polarisation means restricting the vibration to a single plane, so it is possible only when the vibration has a direction transverse to the direction of travel. In a transverse wave the particles move perpendicular to the direction of propagation, and there are infinitely many such perpendicular directions, so one plane can be selected out of them. That is polarisation. In a longitudinal wave, such as sound in air, the particles vibrate along the direction of propagation itself. There is only one such direction, so no plane can be picked out and a longitudinal wave cannot be polarised. The statement asserting the reverse, that longitudinal waves can be polarised while transverse waves cannot, is the false one. Matches option D.
reviewNote: Option (B) is almost certainly a source/OCR corruption: the standard statement is 'a PRESSURE antinode occurs at a displacement node and a pressure node at a displacement antinode'; the stored text reads 'progressive' for 'pressure' in both halves. Key D is unaffected and correct (longitudinal waves cannot be polarised), but the option text should be checked against the printed page.

subject: Physics
stem: A body initially at rest is acted upon by a constant force. The rate of change of its kinetic energy varies:
optA: Linearly with square root of time
solution: The force is constant, so the acceleration \(a = F/m\) is constant. The body starts from rest, so its speed after time \(t\) is \(v = at\). Its kinetic energy is therefore \(K = \frac{1}{2}mv^{2} = \frac{1}{2}m(at)^{2} = \frac{F^{2}t^{2}}{2m}\). Differentiating with respect to time gives the rate of change: \(\frac{dK}{dt} = \frac{F^{2}}{m}t\). Since \(F\) and \(m\) are both fixed, this is a constant multiplied by \(t\), so it grows in direct proportion to \(t\). The same answer follows from power, since the rate of change of kinetic energy is the power delivered: \(P = Fv = F(at) = \frac{F^{2}}{m}t\), which agrees exactly. Note that it is the kinetic energy itself that goes as \(t^{2}\); its rate of change goes as \(t\). Matches option B.

subject: Physics
subtopic: Wave Equation, Speed, and Frequency Bands
stem: A jet plane flies through air with a velocity of 2 Mach. While the velocity of sound is 332 m/s in the air, speed of the plane is:
solution: The Mach number is the ratio of the speed of a body to the speed of sound in the same medium. So speed of body equals Mach number multiplied by speed of sound. Here \(2 \times 332 = 664\) m/s. Check the sizes of the other figures: 166 m/s is half the speed of sound, that is Mach 0.5, and 332 m/s is exactly Mach 1. The value 66.4 km/s is 66400 m/s, which works out to Mach 200, not Mach 2. Matches option D.

subject: Physics
stem: Which one among the following statements is correct?
optA: Convex mirrors are used by doctors to examine oral cavity.
optB: Concave mirrors are used as reflectors.
optC: Convex mirrors are used as reflectors.
optD: Convex mirrors should be used for shaving.
solution: A concave mirror converges light, so a small source placed at its focus sends out a nearly parallel beam. That is precisely what a torch, a motor-car headlight or a searchlight needs, so their reflectors are concave. A convex mirror always diverges the light falling on it and forms a diminished, erect, virtual image with a wide field of view; that suits a rear-view mirror but makes it useless as a reflector. For examining the mouth a doctor or dentist needs a magnified erect image of a nearby tooth, which only a concave mirror held within its focal length can give, and a shaving mirror is concave for the same reason. Matches option B.
reviewNote: [RESOLVED — a second, independent blind derivation reached the printed key (B) without seeing it or the earlier objection, so the key stands. Basis: Reflectors in torches, headlights and searchlights are concave: a source at the focus of a concave mirror sends out a parallel beam. A convex mirror always diverges light and can never do this, so the two convex-reflector and convex-shaving claims fail, and the dentist's mouth mirror is concave because only a concave mirror gives a magnified erect image of a nearby object. Exactly one statement survives, the one naming concave mirrors as reflectors.]

subject: Physics
subtopic: Refraction, Speed of Light and TIR
stem: Light travels in optical fiber irrespective of its shape because it is a device by which signals can be transferred from one location to another. It is based on phenomena of :
solution: An optical fibre has a core of higher refractive index surrounded by a cladding of lower refractive index. Light is launched into the core so that it meets the core-cladding boundary at an angle of incidence greater than the critical angle for that pair of media. At such angles no light is refracted out into the cladding at all; the whole of it is reflected back into the core. The ray then strikes the far wall, again beyond the critical angle, and is reflected again, so it travels the length of the fibre by repeated reflection and follows the fibre round bends. This is why the shape of the fibre does not matter. Simple refraction would let light leak out at each boundary, and neither the bending of light around obstacles nor the restriction of vibration to one plane can confine a beam inside a pipe. Matches option D.

subject: Physics
stem: A man is at rest in the middle of a horizontal plane of perfectly smooth surface of ice. He can move himself to the shore by making use of Newton’s:
optD: First, second and third laws of motion
solution: The ice is perfectly smooth, so there is no friction and the man has nothing to push against; simply walking is impossible because his feet cannot grip. He must therefore throw something he is carrying, such as a shoe or his coat, in the direction away from the shore. While he pushes the object one way, the object pushes back on him with an equal force in the opposite direction, which drives him towards the shore. That equal and opposite reaction is the third law of motion. The first law only tells him he will stay at rest until some force acts, and the second law only relates the force to the acceleration once a force exists; neither supplies the force he needs. Matches option C.

subject: Physics
stem: Which one among the following is the major cause of blurring and unsharp images of objects observed through very large telescope at the extreme limit of magnification?
optB: Poor optical polish achievable on large mirrors.
optD: Varying density of air in the Earth’s atmosphere.
solution: Above every ground-based telescope the atmosphere is broken into cells of air at slightly different temperatures, and therefore at slightly different refractive indices, which are constantly moving and mixing. Light from a star passes through many of these cells and is bent by a slightly different amount every few milliseconds, so the image dances and smears out into a blur. Astronomers call this limit the seeing, and it is what caps the useful magnification: past a certain point extra magnification only enlarges the blur. The other explanations fail on the facts. Large mirrors are figured to a small fraction of a wavelength of light, and telescope drives are computer controlled to a fraction of an arc second, so neither polish nor tracking is the limiting factor on a modern instrument. A smooth, steady change of air density with height does exist, but because it is steady it merely shifts the image to a slightly higher apparent position without making it fuzzy; it is the random, fluctuating part of the density variation, that is the turbulence, that destroys sharpness. Matches option A.
reviewNote: Options (A) 'air turbulence of Earth's atmosphere' and (D) 'varying density of air in the Earth's atmosphere' are near-synonymous descriptions of astronomical seeing. (A) is the standard answer and the key agrees, but the two are weakly discriminated.

subject: Physics
stem: Bats can ascertain distances, directions, nature and size of the obstacles at night. This is possible by reflection of the emitted:
optB: Ultrasonic waves from the distant objects.
optD: Supersonic waves from the distance objects.
solution: A bat sends out pulses of sound above about twenty thousand hertz, that is ultrasound, which is inaudible to us. Each pulse travels outward, strikes an obstacle and returns as an echo. From the time the echo takes to come back the bat judges distance, from the direction it arrives from it judges bearing, and from the strength and quality of the echo it judges size and nature. The waves are therefore produced by the bat and only reflected by the object; the object emits nothing. The word supersonic describes motion faster than sound rather than a kind of wave, so it does not describe what a bat sends out. Matches option A.
reviewNote: [KEY CORRECTED B -> A. Two independent derivations, each made without sight of the printed key, agree against it. This is publisher practice material rather than a past paper, so there is no issued key to preserve. The book prints B. Basis: The waves originate at the bat and are merely turned back by the obstacle, so the emitted waves are the bat's. 'Supersonic' names a speed greater than that of sound, not a class of wave, so both supersonic options are wrong in kind; and an obstacle does not emit anything, which rules out the remaining ultrasonic option.]

subject: Physics
stem: When a moving bus suddenly applies brakes, the passengers sitting in it fall in the forward direction. This can be explained by:
solution: When the brakes are applied, friction acts on the bus and slows it down. The passenger's lower body, which is in contact with the seat, is slowed along with the bus, but no comparable force acts on the upper body, which therefore continues to move forward with the speed it already had. The passenger consequently lurches forward. The tendency of a body to keep moving uniformly unless an external force acts on it is inertia, which is the content of the first law of motion. The second law would be needed to work out how large the deceleration is, and the third law concerns action and reaction pairs; neither is what explains the lurch. Matches option B.

subject: Physics
stem: The material used for electric fuse is an alloy of tin and lead. This alloy should have:
optA: High specific resistance and low melting point.
optB: Low specific resistance and high melting point.
optC: Low specific resistance and low melting point.
optD: High specific resistance and high melting point.
solution: A fuse must melt and break the circuit as soon as the current rises above a safe value, and it must do so before the rest of the wiring is damaged. The heat produced in it is given by \(H = I^{2}Rt\), so for a given current a wire of high specific resistance produces much more heat than ordinary copper wiring of the same size. That heat must then be enough to melt it, which requires a low melting point. A tin and lead alloy is chosen precisely because it satisfies both conditions, melting at a few hundred degrees Celsius. A low specific resistance would leave the fuse cooler than the circuit it is protecting, and a high melting point would let it survive currents that damage the appliance, so either of those choices defeats the purpose of the fuse. Matches option A.

subject: Physics
stem: Suppose you are standing 1 m in front of a plane mirror. What should be the minimum vertical size of the mirror so that you can see your full image in it?
solution: Trace the ray from the top of your head that reaches your eye after reflection. It strikes the mirror at the point exactly halfway in height between your eye and the top of your head, because the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. Similarly the ray from your feet strikes the mirror exactly halfway in height between your eye and your feet. The mirror needs to cover only the strip between those two points. Adding the two halves gives half the distance from your feet to the top of your head, that is \(h/2\). Notice that the distance from the mirror cancels out of this argument entirely, so the 1 m in the question is irrelevant: the same half-height mirror works whether you stand near it or far from it. Matches option C.

subject: Physics
subtopic: Refraction, Speed of Light and TIR
stem: Light travels slower in glass than in air because:
optA: Refractive index of air is less than that of glass.
optB: Refractive index of air is greater than that of glass.
optC: Density of glass is greater than that of air.
optD: Density of glass is less than that of air.
solution: The speed of light in a medium is fixed by that medium's refractive index through \(v = c/n\), where \(c\) is the speed in vacuum. Air has a refractive index of about 1.0003, while ordinary glass has about 1.5. Since the refractive index of air is the smaller of the two, light travels faster in air, and dividing \(c\) by the larger number 1.5 makes the speed in glass roughly two thirds of that in air. The refractive index is the quantity that directly fixes the speed, so it is the reason. Mass density is not: refractive index and mass density need not run together, and there are heavy liquids that slow light less than lighter glasses do. Matches option A.

subject: Physics
subtopic: Magnetism and Magnetic Effects of Current
stem: The lines of force of a uniform magnetic field:
optC: Must be parallel to each other
solution: A field is uniform when it has the same magnitude and the same direction at every point in the region. The direction of the field at a point is the tangent to the line of force there, so if the direction is the same everywhere the lines must all point the same way, that is, they must be parallel. The magnitude is shown by how closely the lines are packed, so equal magnitude everywhere means the lines must also be equally spaced. Lines that converge or diverge would mean the spacing, and hence the strength, changes from place to place, which contradicts uniformity. Lines of force can never intersect in any field at all, uniform or not, because two lines crossing would give the field two different directions at the same point. Matches option C.

subject: Physics
stem: A Jet engine works on the principle of conservation of:
solution: A jet engine takes in air, burns fuel in it and expels the hot gases backwards through a nozzle at very high speed. Those gases carry a large backward momentum. Since no external force acts along the direction of flight during this exchange, the total momentum of the system made up of engine plus exhaust must stay unchanged, so the aircraft acquires an exactly equal forward momentum and is driven ahead. The quantity being conserved is momentum along a straight line, that is linear momentum, not momentum about an axis. Energy is not conserved in the useful sense here, since chemical energy of the fuel is being released, and the mass of the aircraft actually falls as fuel is burnt and ejected. Matches option A.

subject: Physics
stem: The surface temperature of the Sun is nearly :
solution: The visible surface of the Sun is the photosphere, and its temperature is about 5800 K, which to the nearest thousand is nearly 6000 K. This is the temperature that fixes the Sun's colour: a body at roughly 6000 K radiates most strongly in the middle of the visible band, which is why sunlight appears white or slightly yellow. A body at 2000 K would glow dull red and one at 8000 K would look distinctly bluish. Note that this is the surface value only; the core of the Sun is at about 15 million K. Matches option C.

subject: Physics
stem: If the electrical resistance of a typical substance suddenly drops to zero, then the substance is called:
solution: Certain materials, when cooled below a particular temperature called the critical or transition temperature, lose their electrical resistance completely and abruptly. The resistance does not merely become small, it becomes exactly zero, so a current once started in a closed loop of such a material continues without any applied voltage and without dissipating energy. Materials showing this behaviour are called superconductors. Conductors such as copper retain a small resistance at all temperatures, semiconductors have a resistance that falls gradually as temperature rises but never reaches zero, and insulators have very high resistance. Matches option A.

subject: Physics
stem: A spherical air bubble is embedded in a piece of glass. For a ray of light passing through the bubble, it behaves like a:
solution: What a curved surface does to light depends on whether the material inside it has a higher or a lower refractive index than the material outside it. A glass sphere in air has the higher index inside, and it converges light. Here the situation is exactly reversed: the bubble is air, of refractive index about 1, embedded in glass, of refractive index about 1.5, so the refractive index of the bubble relative to its surroundings is less than one. Light entering the bubble therefore bends the opposite way at each surface compared with a glass sphere in air, and a parallel beam is spread apart instead of being brought to a focus. The bubble accordingly behaves as a diverging lens. It is a full sphere with two curved surfaces, not one curved and one flat surface, so neither plano description applies. Matches option B.

subject: Physics
subtopic: Refraction, Speed of Light and TIR
stem: “The stars seem to be higher on the sky than they actually are.” This can be explained by :
solution: The atmosphere is not of uniform density: it grows denser, and so optically denser, as one comes down towards the ground. Light from a star travelling down through it therefore passes continuously from rarer layers into denser ones and is bent towards the normal at each stage, so its path is a curve that is concave towards the Earth. The eye, however, takes no account of this and traces the light back along the straight line in which it finally arrives, so it places the star along that final direction, which is nearer the overhead point than the star's true position. The star thus appears higher in the sky than it really is. This bending of light by the layers of the atmosphere is atmospheric refraction. Matches option A.

subject: Physics
stem: Which one among the following is not a source of renewable energy?
solution: The question asks which one is NOT renewable, so three of the four will be renewable and the odd one out is the answer. A renewable source is one that is naturally replenished as fast as it is used, so it cannot be exhausted by use. Flowing water, sunlight and wind are all continuously renewed by the Sun and the water cycle, so hydroelectricity, solar energy and wind energy are all renewable. A fuel cell is not a source of energy at all; it is a device that converts the chemical energy of a fuel supplied to it, usually hydrogen, directly into electricity. It produces nothing unless that fuel is fed in and consumed, and the hydrogen is at present made mostly from natural gas, which is a fossil fuel. It is therefore a conversion device running on a consumed fuel rather than a renewable source. Matches option C.

subject: Physics
chapter: Fluid Mechanics and Properties of Matter
stem: A liquid rises to a certain length in a capillary tube. The tube is inclined to an angle of 45°. The length of the liquid column will:
solution: In a vertical capillary the liquid rises to a height \(h = \dfrac{2T\cos\theta}{r\rho g}\), where \(T\) is the surface tension, \(\theta\) the angle of contact, \(r\) the radius of the bore and \(\rho\) the density. Tilting the tube changes none of these quantities, so the liquid still climbs to the same VERTICAL height \(h\) above the free surface in the vessel. If the tube now makes an angle of \(45^\circ\) with the vertical, the column measured ALONG the tube has some length \(l\) whose vertical projection must equal \(h\), that is \(l\cos 45^\circ = h\). Hence \(l = \dfrac{h}{\cos 45^\circ} = h\sqrt{2} \approx 1.41\,h\). The vertical rise is unaltered but the length of the liquid column is greater than before. Matches option A.
reviewNote: [RESOLVED — a second, independent blind derivation reached the printed key (A) without seeing it or the earlier objection, so the key stands. Basis: Capillarity fixes the VERTICAL rise, not the length along the tube. The vertical height stays at h because surface tension, contact angle, radius and density are unchanged by tilting; the column measured along the tube is h divided by the cosine of the angle with the vertical, which for 45 degrees is h times root two, about 1.41h. The length increases.]

subject: Physics
stem: Mass of B is four times that of A. B moves with a velocity half than that of A. Then B has:
optA: Kinetic energy equal to that of A
optB: Half the kinetic energy of A
optC: Twice the kinetic energy of A
solution: Let A have mass \(m\) and speed \(v\), so that \(K_{A} = \frac{1}{2}mv^{2}\). Then B has mass \(4m\) and speed \(v/2\), so \(K_{B} = \frac{1}{2}(4m)\left(\frac{v}{2}\right)^{2} = \frac{1}{2} \times 4m \times \frac{v^{2}}{4} = \frac{1}{2}mv^{2}\). The two are therefore equal, and the ratio \(K_{B}/K_{A}\) is exactly 1. The reason is that kinetic energy depends on the square of the speed, so halving the speed divides the energy by 4, and this exactly cancels the factor of 4 gained from the mass. Matches option A.

subject: Physics
stem: In a pressure cooker cooking is faster because the increase in vapour pressure:
solution: A liquid boils at the temperature at which its saturated vapour pressure becomes equal to the pressure acting on its surface. A pressure cooker is sealed, so the steam given off cannot escape and the pressure inside builds up well above atmospheric. The water must then be heated further before its own vapour pressure can rise to match, so boiling is postponed to a higher temperature, about \(120^\circ\)C instead of \(100^\circ\)C. Since the chemical changes of cooking proceed much faster at a higher temperature, the food is cooked in a fraction of the usual time. The specific heat of water is a property of the substance and is not what the raised vapour pressure alters. Matches option D.
reviewNote: [RESOLVED — a second, independent blind derivation reached the printed key (D) without seeing it or the earlier objection, so the key stands. Basis: A liquid boils when its saturated vapour pressure equals the pressure above it. Trapping the steam raises that pressure, so a higher temperature is needed before boiling begins, and water in a cooker boils near 120 degrees Celsius instead of 100. Specific heat is a property of the substance and is not altered here, so the two specific-heat options are irrelevant, and the boiling point rises rather than falls.]

subject: Physics
subtopic: Magnetism and Magnetic Effects of Current
stem: Magnets attract magnetic substances such as iron, nickel, cobalt etc. They can also repel:
solution: Materials respond to a magnetic field in three ways. Ferromagnetic substances such as iron, nickel and cobalt are strongly attracted, and paramagnetic substances such as aluminium and platinum are weakly attracted; in both cases the induced magnetism lies along the applied field, which produces attraction. In diamagnetic substances such as bismuth, copper, water and glass, the applied field induces magnetism in the opposite direction to itself, so these substances are pushed away from the magnet, that is, feebly repelled. This is the only class of matter a magnet repels. There is no substance that is truly non-magnetic; every material falls into one of the three categories above. Matches option C.

subject: Physics
subtopic: Refraction, Speed of Light and TIR
stem: When a ray of light is going from one medium to another, its:
solution: The frequency of a light wave is fixed by the source that produced it and by nothing else. At the boundary between two media the electric field of the wave must match on both sides at every instant, so the oscillations on the far side must keep in step with those on the near side, which means the number of oscillations arriving per second is the number leaving per second. The frequency therefore cannot change. What does change is the speed, since \(v = c/n\). Because \(v = f\lambda\) with \(f\) fixed, the wavelength must change in the same proportion as the speed: entering a denser medium the light slows down and the wavelength shortens. So the wavelength does not stay the same, and the frequency neither rises nor falls. Matches option B.

subject: Chemistry
stem: Which one among the following is the main ingredient in cement?
solution: Ordinary Portland cement is manufactured by burning, in a rotary kiln, a mixture of about four parts limestone to one part clay. The limestone supplies the calcium oxide which combines in the kiln with silica and alumina to form the calcium silicates and aluminates that give set cement its strength, and being roughly four fifths of the charge it is by a wide margin the principal ingredient. Clay contributes the silica and alumina but in a far smaller proportion. Gypsum is not part of the burnt mix at all; a few per cent of it is ground in with the clinker afterwards purely to slow down the setting. Ash is not required. Matches option B.
reviewNote: [RESOLVED — a second, independent blind derivation reached the printed key (B) without seeing it or the earlier objection, so the key stands. Basis: Portland cement is burnt from roughly four parts limestone to one part clay, so limestone is much the largest constituent of the raw mix and supplies the calcium oxide of the calcium silicates. Clay is the minor component, gypsum is added after burning in a few per cent only as a retarder, and ash is not a necessary ingredient.]

subject: Chemistry
stem: Glass is actually
solution: In a crystalline solid the particles are arranged in a regular repeating pattern that extends over long distances, which gives the solid a sharp melting point and definite geometric faces. Glass has no such long-range order; its silicate network is frozen in a disordered arrangement resembling that of a liquid, so it has no sharp melting point but softens gradually over a range of temperature. A solid in this disordered, glass-like state is described as amorphous or vitreous, and the process of forming it is called vitrification, so it is a vitrified solid. It is not built from a lattice of ions like common salt, and elasticity is a mechanical property shared by many solids rather than a description of glass's structure. Matches option D.

subject: Chemistry
subtopic: Acid-Base Theory: Concepts, Oxides and Electrolytes
stem: Solutions in test tubes containing H2O and aqueous NaOH can be differentiated with the help of
solution: Sodium hydroxide solution is a strong base, while water is neutral, so any test that responds to a base will separate them. Red litmus paper is the one that does: dipped in the sodium hydroxide it turns blue, and dipped in water it stays red, giving an immediate visible difference. Blue litmus is useless here, because a base leaves it blue and water also leaves it blue, so both tubes look the same. Sodium carbonate simply dissolves in both tubes with no visible change, since neither liquid is acidic enough to release carbon dioxide from it. Hydrochloric acid neutralises the alkali, but the neutralisation produces only sodium chloride solution and water, which is colourless and clear, so again nothing distinguishes the two tubes to the eye. Matches option A.

subject: Chemistry
subtopic: Acid-Base Theory: Concepts, Oxides and Electrolytes
stem: A student heated some sulphur in a spatula and collected the gas “X”. Which one among the following is correct about “X”?
optA: X is SO2 and it turns moist litmus to blue
optB: X is SO3 and it turns moist litmus to red
optC: X is SO2 and it turns moist litmus to red
optD: X is SO3 and it turns dry litmus to blue
solution: Sulphur heated in air burns with a blue flame to give sulphur dioxide, \(S + O_2 \rightarrow SO_2\). Oxidation as far as sulphur trioxide requires a catalyst such as vanadium pentoxide and does not occur simply on a heated spatula, so the gas collected is the dioxide. Sulphur dioxide is an acidic oxide, and to act on litmus it must first dissolve in water, \(SO_2 + H_2O \rightarrow H_2SO_3\), giving sulphurous acid. That acid turns blue litmus red. Dry litmus paper shows no change at all, because without water no acid can be formed, and no acidic oxide can ever turn litmus blue. Matches option C.
reviewNote: [RESOLVED — a second, independent blind derivation reached the printed key (C) without seeing it or the earlier objection, so the key stands. Basis: Sulphur burning in air on a spatula gives sulphur dioxide; the further oxidation to the trioxide needs a catalyst and does not happen here, which disposes of both trioxide options. Sulphur dioxide is an ACIDIC oxide, so it turns moist blue litmus red, not blue, and it needs the moisture in order to form sulphurous acid, so dry litmus shows nothing.]

subject: Chemistry
subtopic: Common Acids: Names, Formulas and Uses
stem: Human stomach produces acid ‘X’ which helps in digestion of food. Acid ‘X’ is:
solution: The gastric glands in the wall of the stomach secrete hydrochloric acid, which makes the contents of the stomach strongly acidic at a pH of about 1.5 to 3.5. This acidity serves two purposes in digestion: it kills most bacteria swallowed with the food, and it provides the acidic medium in which the enzyme pepsin becomes active and can begin breaking proteins down. The other acids named belong elsewhere: acetic acid is the acid of vinegar, methanoic or formic acid is found in ant stings, and citric acid occurs in citrus fruits. None of these is secreted by the stomach. Matches option C.

subject: Chemistry
subtopic: Practical Applications: Health, Food and Lab Methods
stem: When concentrated H2SO4 spilts on the surface, it should be immediately cleaned:
solution: Spilt concentrated sulphuric acid must be neutralised, and solid sodium carbonate does this safely because it is a mild base that reacts with the acid to give a harmless salt, water and carbon dioxide gas: \(\mathrm{Na_2CO_3 + H_2SO_4 \rightarrow Na_2SO_4 + H_2O + CO_2}\). The fizzing of the escaping gas even shows when the reaction is complete, and any excess carbonate left behind is harmless. Adding cold water is dangerous rather than helpful: concentrated sulphuric acid releases a great deal of heat when it mixes with water, and poured onto a spill the water can boil at once and spatter the acid outwards. Wiping with a cloth simply chars the cloth and spreads the acid, and barium chloride merely precipitates barium sulphate while leaving hydrochloric acid behind, so the surface is still acidic. Matches option C.

subject: Chemistry
subtopic: Types of Reactions: Combination, Decomposition, Displacement
stem: Iron nails are dipped into blue copper sulphate solution. After some time iron nails are
optA: Dissolved and blue colour is discharged.
optB: Dissolved but blue colour is not discharged.
optC: Not dissolved and blue colour is not discharged.
optD: Not dissolved but blue colour is discharged.
solution: Iron lies above copper in the reactivity series, so iron displaces copper from a solution of its salt: \(\mathrm{Fe + CuSO_4 \rightarrow FeSO_4 + Cu}\). Two things follow, and both are visible. The iron goes into solution as iron sulphate, so the nails are eaten away and lose weight, and a reddish brown deposit of copper collects on them. At the same time the blue colour of the solution, which is due to the copper ions in it, fades away as those ions are removed, and it is replaced by the pale green of iron sulphate. So the nails dissolve and the blue colour is discharged; the two changes happen together because they are two sides of the same displacement reaction. Matches option A.
reviewNote: Dedup verdict was 'maybe' against bank row d3cd724b-cfbc-44e9-90cf-5e780d509499 ('When Iron nails are dipped in Copper Sulphate solution, the color of the solution...'): same experiment, but the bank row asks for the resulting colour while this one asks about dissolution and decolourisation. Filed as new per the dedup rules.

subject: Chemistry
stem: A student by chance mixed acetone with alcohol. This mixture of acetone and alcohol can be separated by:
solution: Acetone and alcohol are both liquids and they mix completely, forming a single clear layer. That immediately rules out filtration, which separates an insoluble solid from a liquid, and a separating funnel, which needs two liquids that refuse to mix and settle into distinct layers. Fractional crystallisation separates solids of differing solubility from a solution, so it does not apply either. What does distinguish the two liquids is their boiling points: acetone boils at about 56 degrees Celsius and ethanol at about 78 degrees Celsius, a gap of about 22 degrees. Because this gap is fairly small, simple distillation would carry over a mixture of both vapours; a fractionating column is needed, in which the rising vapour repeatedly condenses and re-evaporates so that the lower-boiling acetone is progressively enriched and distils over first. Matches option D.

subject: Chemistry
stem:
Which of the statements given below is/are correct? Permanent hardness of water is due to the presence of soluble:
1. Chloride of calcium
2. Bicarbonate of calcium
3. Sulphate of magnesium
4. Bicarbonate of magnesium Select the correct answer using the code given below:
solution: Hardness of water is caused by dissolved calcium and magnesium salts, and it is classified by whether boiling removes it. Temporary hardness is due to the bicarbonates of calcium and magnesium; on boiling these decompose to insoluble carbonates which settle out, so the hardness disappears. That disposes of statements 2 and 4, which name bicarbonates and therefore belong to temporary hardness. Permanent hardness is due to the chlorides and sulphates of calcium and magnesium, which are unaffected by boiling and must be removed chemically, for instance by washing soda or by an ion exchange resin. Statement 1 names calcium chloride and statement 3 names magnesium sulphate, and both of these are indeed causes of permanent hardness. So statements 1 and 3 are the correct pair. Matches option B.

Needs line-splitting in the parser. Key B (1 and 3) is correct - permanent hardness is due to chlorides and sulphates, not bicarbonates.

subject: Chemistry
stem:
Which of the following statements about diamond are correct?
1. It is used as a gem in jewellery because of its ability to reflect light.
2. It is a good conductor of electricity.
3. It is used for cutting glass, marble stones and other hard materials.
4. It is used for drilling of rocks Select the correct answer using the code given below:
solution: Take the statements one at a time. Diamond has a very high refractive index and a correspondingly small critical angle, so light entering a cut stone is totally internally reflected several times before emerging, which produces the brilliance that makes it valued as a gem; statement 1 stands. In diamond every carbon atom is joined to four neighbours by covalent bonds, so all four of its valence electrons are locked into bonding and none is free to carry a current. Diamond is therefore an insulator, not a conductor of electricity, and statement 2 is false. Note in passing that diamond is an excellent conductor of heat, which is the property statement 2 confuses this with. Diamond is also the hardest natural substance known, which is exactly why it is used to cut glass and marble and to tip rock drilling bits, so statements 3 and 4 both stand. The correct combination is 1, 3 and 4. Matches option A.
reviewNote: Rule 1: the four numbered statements about diamond are flattened onto one line. Key A (1, 3 and 4) is correct - diamond is a poor conductor of electricity, so statement 2 is false.

subject: Chemistry
stem: Which one among the following methods is not effective in removing arsenic from contaminated ground water?
solution: The question asks which method does NOT work, so the answer is the one ineffective method. Arsenic in groundwater is present as dissolved arsenite and arsenate compounds, which are not volatile. When the water is boiled, only the water evaporates while the arsenic compounds stay behind, so boiling actually raises the concentration of arsenic in whatever water is left and makes matters worse rather than better. Boiling is effective only against germs, not against dissolved chemical contaminants. The other three methods do remove arsenic: reverse osmosis forces the water through a membrane that holds back the dissolved arsenic ions, ion exchange swaps the arsenate ions for harmless ions held on a resin, and coagulation with a salt such as ferric chloride makes the arsenic adsorb onto flocs of iron hydroxide which are then filtered off. Matches option A.

subject: Chemistry
stem: Bronze is often used to make statues and medals whereas brass is used in making utensils, scientific apparatus and cartridges. Both brass and bronze are copper containing alloys, yet they differ in their chemical composition for additionally containing :
optA: Zinc in brass and tin in bronze
optB: Chromium in brass and nickel in bronze
optC: Nickel in brass and tin in bronze
optD: Iron in brass and nickel in bronze
solution: Both alloys are based on copper, and it is the second metal that distinguishes them. Brass is copper alloyed with zinc, typically around 70 per cent copper to 30 per cent zinc; the zinc makes it harder than copper, easy to machine and cast, and gives it a bright yellow colour, which suits it to utensils, instrument fittings and cartridge cases. Bronze is copper alloyed with tin, typically around 90 per cent copper to 10 per cent tin; tin makes it harder still, resistant to corrosion and able to reproduce fine detail when cast, which is why statues and medals are made of it. So the added metal is zinc in brass and tin in bronze. Chromium and nickel belong to steels rather than to these two alloys, and iron is an impurity in copper alloys rather than a deliberate ingredient. Matches option A.

subject: Chemistry
stem:
Which of the statements about glass are correct?
1. Glass is a super cooled liquid having infinite viscosity.
2. Violet coloured glass is obtained by adding MnO2
3. Glass is a man made silicate
4. Glass is a crystalline substance Select the correct answer using the code given below:
solution: Work through the statements. Glass has no orderly crystal lattice; its particles are frozen in the disordered arrangement of a liquid, which is why it softens gradually instead of melting at a sharp temperature. It is therefore described as a supercooled liquid whose viscosity is so enormous that it holds its shape indefinitely, and statement 1 stands, while statement 4, which calls it crystalline, is plainly false. Since statement 4 is false, any combination containing it can be discarded at once. Glass is manufactured by fusing sand, which is silica, with soda and lime, giving a man-made silicate, so statement 3 stands. Coloured glasses are made by adding small quantities of metal oxides to the melt, and manganese dioxide is the one that gives a violet or amethyst tint, just as cobalt oxide gives blue and chromium oxide gives green; so statement 2 stands as well. The correct combination is therefore 1, 2 and 3. Matches option C.
reviewNote: Rule 1: the four numbered statements about glass are flattened onto one line. Key C (1, 2 and 3) is correct - glass is amorphous, so statement 4 is false.

subject: Biology
stem: Sandalwood tree is considered a:
solution: A total parasite has no chlorophyll of its own and must draw everything, food included, from its host. Sandalwood is not like that: it is a tree with ordinary green leaves and it photosynthesises its own food perfectly well. What it cannot do is gather enough water and mineral salts by itself, so its roots put out sucking structures called haustoria which fasten onto the roots of neighbouring host plants and tap their water and minerals. Because it takes only part of its requirements, and takes them through the root, it is classed as a partial root parasite, also called a root hemiparasite. It is not a stem parasite, since the attachment is underground at the roots and not on the host's shoot. Matches option D.

subject: Biology
stem: Which one among the following statements about stomach is not correct ?
optA: Stomach acts as a temporary reservoir.
optB: Stomach mixes food with gastric juice.
optC: Stomach secretes lipase and amylase in gastric juice.
optD: Rate of stomach emptying depends on the type of food.
solution: The question asks which statement is NOT correct, so three of the four describe the stomach truly and one does not. The stomach does hold a meal for some hours and release it into the duodenum a little at a time, so it acts as a temporary reservoir. Its muscular walls do churn the food and mix it thoroughly with gastric juice to form chyme. The rate at which it empties does depend on what has been eaten, a fatty meal leaving most slowly and a liquid carbohydrate meal fastest. Gastric juice, however, consists of hydrochloric acid, pepsinogen, mucus, intrinsic factor and a small quantity of gastric lipase; it contains no amylase whatever. Starch digestion is begun by salivary amylase in the mouth and completed by pancreatic amylase in the small intestine. The statement that the stomach secretes amylase is therefore the incorrect one. Matches option C.
reviewNote: [RESOLVED — a second, independent blind derivation reached the printed key (C) without seeing it or the earlier objection, so the key stands. Basis: Polarity: the stem asks for the statement that is NOT correct, so three are true and one is false. Reservoir function, mixing with gastric juice and food-dependent emptying are all true. Gastric juice contains hydrochloric acid, pepsinogen, mucus, intrinsic factor and a little gastric lipase, but NO amylase; starch is handled by salivary and pancreatic amylase. That claim is the false one.]

subject: Biology
stem: Which one of the following organs breaks fat to produce cholesterol ?
solution: Cholesterol is not chiefly taken in with food; most of it is manufactured within the body, and the liver is the organ that does this. The liver takes up fatty acids, breaks them down and uses the resulting two-carbon units to build cholesterol, and it also packages the cholesterol into lipoproteins for transport in the blood and converts surplus cholesterol into bile salts. The intestine absorbs digested fat and the bile made by the liver assists that absorption, but the intestine is not where cholesterol is synthesised in quantity. The lungs deal with exchange of gases and the kidneys with filtering the blood and forming urine; neither has any role in fat breakdown. Matches option B.

subject: Geography
chapter: Earth in Space, Maps and Coordinates
stem:
Consider the following statements about comets:
1. Most comets have elongated elliptical orbits that take them close to the Sun for a part of their orbit, and then out into the further reaches of the Solar System for the remainder.
2. If a comet is travelling fast enough, it may leave the Solar System.
Which of the following statements is/are correct?
solution: Statement 1 describes the orbit of a typical comet correctly. Comets move on highly eccentric ellipses, so they spend a short part of each orbit near the Sun, where the heat drives off gas and dust and produces the visible tail, and the far longer remainder out in the cold outer Solar System where they are inert. Halley's comet is the familiar example, sweeping in past the Earth's orbit and back out beyond Neptune. Statement 2 is also correct. Whether a body stays bound to the Sun depends on whether its speed is below the escape speed at its distance. A comet perturbed by the gravity of a large planet can be pushed above that speed, and its path then becomes a hyperbola instead of a closed ellipse, so it makes one pass and departs the Solar System for good. Both statements are therefore correct. Matches option C.
reviewNote: Rule 1: the two numbered statements are flattened onto one line. Key C is correct. Filed to Geography/Planets and Solar System following the bank's dominant home for solar-system objects (7 rows there against 4 in Physics/Astronomy and Space).

subject: Biology
stem: An individual whose blood type is B may in an emergency donate blood to a person whose blood type is:
solution: Transfusion is governed by the antigens on the donor's red cells and the antibodies in the recipient's plasma; the danger is that the recipient's antibodies attack the donated cells and clump them. A donor of group B has the B antigen on his red cells, so his blood may safely be given only to a recipient whose plasma carries no anti-B antibody. Group B people carry anti-A but not anti-B, and group AB people carry neither antibody, so both can receive it. Group A people carry anti-B in their plasma and group O people carry both anti-A and anti-B, so donated B cells would be attacked in either of them. The safe recipients are therefore groups B and AB. Matches option D.

chapter: Earth in Space, Maps and Coordinates
stem:
Which of the following statements is/are correct?
1. In comparison to the Jupiter, planet Earth displays eclipses more frequently
2. On Mars, only partial solar eclipses are possible Select the correct answer using the code given below:
solution: Take the two statements in turn. Jupiter has four large moons, and the innermost of them completes an orbit in less than two days, so their shadows sweep across the planet almost without a break; solar eclipses are an everyday occurrence there, whereas the Earth sees only two to five solar eclipses in a year. The claim that the Earth has them more often than Jupiter is therefore wrong. Mars, by contrast, has only two very small moons, Phobos and Deimos. Even Phobos, the larger and nearer of the two, subtends an angle appreciably smaller than that of the Sun as seen from Mars, so it can never hide the solar disc completely; Deimos is smaller still and merely crosses the Sun as a dot. Only partial eclipses can occur on Mars, so the second statement is correct while the first is not. Matches option B.
reviewNote: [RESOLVED — a second, independent blind derivation reached the printed key (B) without seeing it or the earlier objection, so the key stands. Basis: Statement 1 is FALSE: Jupiter's four Galilean moons, the innermost of which orbits in under two days, throw shadows on the planet almost continuously, so eclipses there are far more frequent than the two to five solar eclipses the Earth sees in a year. Statement 2 is TRUE: Phobos and Deimos are both too small in angular size to cover the solar disc from Mars, so no total eclipse is possible there.]

subject: Biology
stem: Venkataraman Ramakrishnan was jointly awarded Nobel Prize in Chemistry in the year 2009 for the:
optB: Studies of the structure and function of the ribosome.
optC: Palladium catalyzed cross couplings in organic synthesis.
optD: Work in the area of olefin metathesis.
solution: Venkatraman Ramakrishnan shared the 2009 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with Thomas Steitz and Ada Yonath. Their work mapped the atomic structure of the ribosome, the particle on which a cell assembles proteins by reading the genetic message, using X-ray crystallography, and showed how that structure carries out the job. The result mattered practically as well, because many antibiotics work by blocking bacterial ribosomes and the structures showed exactly where and how they bind. The other citations named belong to different prizes: electron transfer theory was recognised in 1992, palladium catalysed cross coupling in 2010, and olefin metathesis in 2005. Matches option B.
reviewNote: Filed by DISCIPLINE rather than as an awards item, following the bank precedent that the 1962 DNA Nobel question sits in Biology/Genetics and Evolution/Heredity and DNA rather than in Current Affairs. The testable fact here is ribosome structure and function.

subject: Biology
stem: Which one among the following statements regarding cell is not correct?
optA: Shape and size of cells are related to specific function.
optC: Each cell has its own capacity to perform.
optD: Same type of cells are present in all body tissues.
solution: The question asks which statement is NOT correct, so look for the false one. A tissue is by definition a group of cells of similar type doing a particular job, and different tissues are built from quite different cells: long branched nerve cells for carrying impulses, long contractile muscle fibres for movement, flat closely packed epithelial cells for lining surfaces, and biconcave red cells for carrying oxygen. So it is simply not true that the same type of cell is present in all body tissues, and that is the statement being sought. The other three are sound. Shape and size do follow function, as the long nerve cell shows. Some cells do change shape, the white blood cell being the standard example as it crawls and engulfs bacteria. And each cell does carry out its own activities of respiration, nutrition and excretion, which is why the cell is called the structural and functional unit of life. Matches option D.

subject: Biology
stem: Which one among the following Indian scientists proposed a theory for long distance transport of water in plants?
solution: Long distance transport of water from root to leaf, the ascent of sap, was explained in the west by the cohesion tension theory. The Indian contribution to the problem came from Jagadish Chandra Bose, who proposed the pulsation theory: he held that the living cells of the innermost cortical layer pulsate rhythmically and so pump water upward through the plant, and he devised instruments to record these pulsations. Of the other names, Birbal Sahni is remembered as the founder of Indian palaeobotany, Panchanan Maheshwari for his work on the embryology of flowering plants and tissue culture, and N.S. Parihar for the study of bryophytes and pteridophytes. None of the three worked on water transport. Matches option A.
reviewNote: [RESOLVED — a second, independent blind derivation reached the printed key (A) without seeing it or the earlier objection, so the key stands. Basis: Jagadish Chandra Bose put forward the pulsation theory of the ascent of sap, holding that rhythmic pulsation of living cortical cells drives water upward. Birbal Sahni worked on palaeobotany, Panchanan Maheshwari on angiosperm embryology and N.S. Parihar on bryophytes and pteridophytes, none of which concerns water transport.]

subject: Geography
chapter: Earth in Space, Maps and Coordinates
stem: To a perpendicular to the plane of ecliptic, Earth’s axis of rotation makes an angle of 23 1/2 degrees. Had this angle been zero degree, which one among the following would result?
optA: There would have been no seasons
optB: The lengths of day and night would have been the same throughout the year
optC: The length of day and night would have been the same all over the Earth
solution: The inclination of the axis is what makes the Sun's vertical rays travel back and forth between the tropics through the year. If that angle were zero the Sun would remain vertically above the equator at all times, so the distribution of heating would never change from month to month and there would be no succession of seasons. With an upright axis the circle of illumination, which separates the lit half of the Earth from the dark half, would pass through both poles at every moment and so would cut every parallel of latitude into two equal halves. Each place would therefore be in daylight for twelve hours and in darkness for twelve, the same at every latitude and the same on every day of the year. All three of the stated consequences hold together. Matches option D.
reviewNote: [RESOLVED — a second, independent blind derivation reached the printed key (D) without seeing it or the earlier objection, so the key stands. Basis: Zero tilt keeps the Sun vertically over the equator all year, so seasons disappear; the circle of illumination then passes through both poles at all times, halving every parallel of latitude, which makes day and night twelve hours each everywhere and on every date. All three listed consequences follow, so the combined option is the answer.]

subject: Geography
stem: The exceptionally high and low tides that occur at the time of the new moon or the full moon when the Sun, the Moon and the Earth are approximately aligned is called
solution: Tides are raised by the gravitational pull of the Moon and, more weakly, of the Sun. At new moon and at full moon the Sun, the Moon and the Earth lie roughly in a straight line, so the two pulls act along the same line and reinforce each other. The combined tide-raising force is then at its greatest, producing unusually high high tides and unusually low low tides. These are called spring tides, twice in each lunar month; the name has nothing to do with the season and comes from the sense of water springing up. When the Moon is at first or third quarter the Sun and Moon pull at right angles and partly cancel, giving the feeble neap tides. A diurnal tide describes how many tides occur in a day, not their size. Matches option A.

subject: Geography
stem: Which is the general direction of cyclones formed in the Bay of Bengal?
solution: Cyclones in the Bay of Bengal form in tropical latitudes, and in that belt the prevailing winds in which they are embedded are the tropical easterlies, or trade winds, which blow from east to west. A cyclone is carried along by the broad flow surrounding it, so these storms travel generally westward, usually curving somewhat north of west as they go, and strike the eastern coast of India in Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu or Bangladesh. That westward track is why storms forming in the middle of the Bay threaten the Indian coast rather than moving away from it. Matches option A.

subject: Geography
subtopic: Indian Rivers, Lakes and Water Bodies
stem: The Narmada River in the Peninsular plateau flows westward with a remarkably straight channel. It is because the:
optA: Slope gradient in this part controls the river channel pattern.
optB: River carries a huge amount of water which has created a straight channel course.
optC: River forms the boundary between the Central Highlands and the Deccan Plateau.
optD: River flows through the trough of a rift valley inclined westward.
solution: The Narmada does not flow in a valley it cut for itself. It occupies a rift valley, a long narrow trough where a block of the Earth's crust has sunk between two parallel faults, with the Vindhya range standing along the northern fault and the Satpura along the southern one. Because the river is simply following a fracture line in the crust, its course is set by the geological structure rather than by erosion, and fractures of this kind run straight; the trough is also tilted towards the west, which is why a peninsular river flows west into the Arabian Sea instead of east like the Godavari and the Krishna. A slope alone would not produce so straight a channel, since rivers on open slopes meander freely, and the volume of water a river carries does not straighten its course. It is true that the Narmada separates the Central Highlands from the Deccan Plateau, but that is a consequence of its position along the trough, not an explanation of why the channel is straight. Matches option D.

subject: Geography
stem: No trees are found in Tundra biome near polar region of northern hemisphere. This is due to:
optB: Frozen ice beneath the surface soil (permafrost) restricts root growth
optC: Less wind movement and inadequate sunlight
optD: Low temperature which restricts development of reproductive organs
solution: Below the thin surface layer of tundra soil lies permafrost, ground that stays frozen solid throughout the year. Only the topmost few centimetres thaw in the brief summer, so a root cannot penetrate more than that shallow depth. A tree needs to send roots deep both to anchor a tall trunk against the wind and to reach enough water and nutrients to supply a large crown, and the frozen layer makes this impossible; the frozen ground also blocks drainage, leaving the thin thawed layer waterlogged and short of oxygen. Only shallow rooted mosses, lichens, sedges and dwarf shrubs can therefore survive, and the treeless tundra results. Snow does not stop plants respiring, and it is the frozen subsoil rather than a shortage of wind that is decisive. Matches option B.

subject: Geography
stem: Why the summer monsoon winds blow from South Western direction in the Northern hemisphere?
optA: The general direction of wind from the Indian Ocean is South Western.
optB: The presence of the doldrums around the equator.
optC: The low-pressure conditions in North-West India.
optD: Due to the effect of Coriolis force.
solution: In the southern hemisphere summer monsoon season the winds concerned begin as the south-east trade winds blowing towards the equator. Drawn on by intense low pressure over north-western India, they cross the equator into the northern hemisphere. On crossing, the sense of the Earth's rotational deflection reverses: in the northern hemisphere the Coriolis force turns a moving air mass to its right. Winds arriving from the south-east are therefore swung round to arrive from the south-west, which is why the rain-bearing current reaches India as the south-west monsoon. Note what each explanation accounts for. The low pressure over north-western India explains why the winds blow towards India at all, but not the compass direction from which they arrive; only the deflection explains that they come specifically from the south-west rather than the south-east. Matches option D.

subject: Geography
chapter: Earth in Space, Maps and Coordinates
stem: If the Earth’s axis were perpendicular to the plane of its orbit, which one among the following would not have happened?
optA: The North pole will always lie in dark.
optB: Days and nights would be equal throughout the year.
optC: No change of seasons will take place.
optD: The Sun will be perpendicular to the equator.
solution: An axis perpendicular to the plane of the orbit means the axis has no inclination at all, and the question asks which of the listed effects would then NOT occur. With no tilt the Sun stays vertically over the equator throughout the year, so the Sun is indeed always perpendicular to the equator and the pattern of heating never changes, which abolishes the seasons. The circle of illumination would pass through both poles at all times and cut every parallel in half, so days and nights would be equal, of twelve hours each, all through the year. Those three would all come about. At the North Pole, however, the Sun would then lie permanently on the horizon, giving continuous twilight rather than continuous darkness. The long polar night that the pole actually experiences exists only because the axis is tilted away from the Sun for half the year, so removing the tilt removes the polar night as well. A North Pole always lying in darkness is the one consequence that would not follow. Matches option A.
reviewNote: [RESOLVED — a second, independent blind derivation reached the printed key (A) without seeing it or the earlier objection, so the key stands. Basis: Polarity: an axis perpendicular to the orbital plane means ZERO tilt, and the stem asks which effect would NOT follow. Equal day and night through the year, no seasons, and the Sun standing over the equator all follow. At the North Pole the Sun would sit permanently on the horizon, giving perpetual twilight; the six-month polar night is itself produced by the tilt, so removing the tilt removes it. Permanent darkness at the pole is the one thing that would not happen.]
