subject: Geography
chapter: Indian Geography — Economy, Resources and Transport
subtopic: Agriculture, Crops, Soils and Land Use
stem: Which one among the following is the best reason for the marked increase in the agricultural production in India in the past decades?
optA: Increases in the area under cultivation.
optB: Conversion of barren land into agricultural land.
optC: Use of improved agricultural methods and technologies.
optD: Priority status given by the successive governments to agricultural sector over the industry sector.
solution: India's net sown area has been close to its limit for decades and has barely grown, since almost all land fit for the plough is already under it; so extra output cannot be explained by cultivating more ground, and there is little barren land left that can be converted cheaply. What has changed is the yield obtained from each hectare. Since the Green Revolution, high yielding varieties of wheat and rice, chemical fertilisers, assured irrigation from tube wells and canals, pesticides, tractors and better storage have together raised production per hectare several times over, and the same land now grows two or three crops a year instead of one. Improved methods and technology are therefore the main reason. Priority in government policy has helped fund those inputs, but by itself a budget allocation grows no grain; it is the technology it paid for that did. Matches option C.

subject: Geography
chapter: Earth's Structure, Landforms and Geological Time
stem: Which of the following statements regarding the Deccan Traps is/are correct? (a) Intense volcanic activity in the form of fissure eruption took place towards the end of Cretaceous period. (b) The volcanic lava spread out in horizontal sheets. (c) The regur soil found here is rich in nitrogen. Select the correct answer using the codes given below:
solution: Take the three statements one at a time. The first is correct. The Deccan Traps were formed by an outpouring of lava through long fissures in the crust rather than through central vents, and this activity belongs to the close of the Cretaceous period, about 66 million years ago. The second is correct as well, and it follows from the kind of lava involved. The lava was basaltic, meaning poor in silica and therefore very fluid, so it could not pile up into steep cones; instead it flooded far across the surface and congealed as nearly horizontal sheets laid one upon another. Successive sheets weather back at different rates, giving the step-like terraces from which the name 'traps' is taken. The third statement is not correct, and it reverses a well-known property. The black soil, or regur, that forms when this basalt weathers is indeed fertile, and it is rich in lime, iron, magnesia, alumina and potash, and it holds moisture well, which is why cotton grows on it. But it is markedly deficient in nitrogen, in phosphorus and in humus, which is precisely why nitrogenous fertiliser has to be added when the land is cropped. So the first and second statements are correct and the third is not. Matches option A.
reviewNote: [KEY CORRECTED B -> A. A third derivation, made without sight of the key or of the earlier attempts, independently reached the same answer as an earlier blind pass. Two independent derivations against the printed key. This is publisher practice material, not a past paper, so there is no issued key to preserve; the book prints B. Basis: The stem labels its statements with letters while the options number them, but the correspondence is one to one and unambiguous. The first statement is correct: the Deccan Traps were built by fissure eruptions at the close of the Cretaceous, about 66 million years ago. The second is correct: the lava was basaltic and highly fluid, so it flooded outward and solidified as nearly horizontal sheets stacked one on another, producing the step-like terraces from which 'traps' takes its name. The third is false and is the standard trap: regur, the black cotton soil derived from this basalt, is rich in lime, iron, magnesia, alumina and potash but is deficient in nitrogen, phosphorus and humus. So the first two are correct and the third is not.]

subject: Geography
subtopic: Forests and Natural Vegetation of India
stem:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Himalayan vegetation varies according to both altitude and climatic conditions.
2. There are mainly two types of tropical forests that are found in the Himalayas— the tropical rainforests and the tropical deciduous forests.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
solution: Statement 1 is correct and is the governing principle of Himalayan vegetation. Climbing the Himalayas is much like travelling from the equator towards the pole: temperature falls with height, so the plant cover changes in bands, from tropical forest in the foothills through subtropical pine and temperate deciduous and coniferous forest to alpine meadow and finally bare snow. Rainfall also varies, being far heavier in the eastern Himalayas than in the drier western ranges, so at the same altitude the two ends of the range carry different forest. Both altitude and climate therefore govern the vegetation. Statement 2 describes the lowest of those belts. In the foothills and terai below about a thousand metres the climate is tropical, and the forest there falls into two main kinds: tropical evergreen rainforest where the rain is heavy and spread through the year, chiefly in the eastern Himalayas, and tropical deciduous forest, of which sal is typical, where the rainfall is more seasonal. Both statements are therefore correct. Matches option C.
reviewNote: Rule 1: the two numbered statements are flattened onto one line. Key C is correct.

subject: Geography
chapter: Indian Geography — Economy, Resources and Transport
subtopic: Agriculture, Crops, Soils and Land Use
stem: Which one among the following is not a reason for practising tank irrigation in the Peninsular India?
optA: The undulating relief and hard rocks.
optB: Little percolation of rain water due to impervious rock structure.
optC: Most of the rivers of Peninsular India are perennial.
optD: There are many streams which become torrential during rainy season.
solution: Tank irrigation is adopted where water has to be ponded on the surface because canals and wells are difficult to build. In the Peninsula the relief is undulating, so water collects naturally in depressions while long canals are costly to cut; the underlying rock is hard crystalline rock that is impervious, so rain water does not percolate down to recharge groundwater and must be held above ground; and the rain-fed streams run torrentially through the monsoon and dry up afterwards, so their water has to be stored while it is available. Each of those is a genuine reason for building tanks. The remaining statement claims the Peninsular rivers are perennial, which is untrue: the Godavari, Krishna and Cauvery are rain-fed and their discharge falls sharply once the monsoon withdraws. It is also self-defeating as a reason, because perennial rivers would reduce the need for tanks rather than create it. Matches option C.

subject: Geography
subtopic: Location, Extent and Frontiers of India
stem:
Identify from the following states of India through which the Tropic of Cancer passes and arrange them from east to west:
1. Gujarat
2. West Bengal
3. Uttar Pradesh
4. Jharkhand
5. Madhya Pradesh
6. Bihar
7. Chhattisgarh Select the correct answer using the code given below:
solution: The Tropic of Cancer crosses eight Indian states: Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura and Mizoram. Uttar Pradesh and Bihar lie north of it and are therefore eliminated at once, which rules out both sequences that open with Uttar Pradesh. Of the five states in the list that do qualify, order them by longitude and read from east to west: West Bengal (the Tropic crosses it near Krishnanagar, about 88 degrees East), then Jharkhand (about 85 degrees East), then Chhattisgarh (about 82 degrees East), then Madhya Pradesh (about 78 degrees East), then Gujarat (about 72 degrees East). That is 2-4-7-5-1. The sequence that places Madhya Pradesh before Chhattisgarh reverses two of these and fails. Matches option B.
reviewNote: Rule 1: the seven numbered States are flattened onto one line. Dedup verdict was 'maybe' against bank row 634c920f-d645-4f02-9f57-d047cc9484aa ('The Tropic of Cancer does not pass through which one of the following States?'): same underlying fact set, but the bank row asks for an exclusion and this one asks for an east-to-west ordering. Filed as new. Key B (2-4-7-5-1) is correct.

subject: Geography
stem: Hot deserts like Sahara, Arabia etc, receive very negligible amount of rainfall. This is because they _______.
optA: Do not receive moisture-bearing wind from the oceans
optB: Are the most rocky and barren areas of the Earth
optC: Are located on the tropical high-pressure belt of the atmosphere
optD: are not on the path of the monsoons
solution: Rain can fall only where air rises, cools and its moisture condenses. The Sahara, Arabia and the other hot deserts lie in a belt close to the tropics into which air that rose over the equator, having travelled poleward at a great height and lost its moisture on the way, sinks back towards the surface. Descending air is compressed and therefore warmed, and warm air can hold more moisture rather than less, so it moves further from saturation as it comes down and cloud cannot form at all. This permanent belt of subtropical high pressure is what keeps these lands almost rainless. Their bare and rocky surface is a result of the long-continued aridity rather than a cause of it, and the fact that moist onshore winds do not reach them is itself a consequence of the same pressure and wind pattern, so it is a symptom rather than the underlying reason. Matches option C.
reviewNote: [KEY CORRECTED A -> C. Two independent derivations, each made without sight of the printed key, agree against it. This is publisher practice material rather than a past paper, so there is no issued key to preserve. The book prints A. Basis: Rainfall requires ascending, cooling air. The hot deserts lie in the subtropical high-pressure belt where air that rose at the equator descends, warming by compression and so drying, which prevents condensation. Rockiness is a consequence of aridity rather than its cause, and the absence of onshore moist winds is itself produced by the same pressure pattern, so neither is the underlying reason.]

subject: Geography
chapter: Earth in Space, Maps and Coordinates
stem: The latitude is the angular distance of a point on the Earth’s surface, north or South of the equator as measured from the ______.
optB: Tropic of Cancer or of Capricorn
solution: Latitude is an angle, and every angle must be measured at a vertex. Join the place to the centre of the Earth, and join the point on the equator on the same meridian to the centre of the Earth; the angle between these two radii, formed at the centre, is the latitude of the place. The equator is the reference circle from which the count begins, and the question has already said the distance is reckoned north or south of the equator, so naming it again supplies no new information. The poles are merely where that angle reaches ninety degrees. The point from which the angular distance is measured is the centre of the Earth. Matches option A.

subject: Polity
chapter: Government Structure — Parliament, Judiciary and Constitutional Bodies
stem: When an ordinary Bill is referred to a joint sitting of both the Houses of Indian Parliament. It has to be passed by a:
optA: Simple majority of the total number of members of both the Houses present and voting.
optB: Two-third majority of the total number of members of both the Houses.
optC: Simple majority of the total number of members of both the Houses.
optD: Two-third majority of the total number of members of both the Houses present and voting.
solution: Article 108(4) provides that at a joint sitting the Bill shall be passed by a majority of the total number of members of both Houses present and voting. Two things settle the choice. First, the majority required is a simple one, not two-thirds; a special two-thirds majority belongs to a Constitution Amendment Bill under Article 368, not to an ordinary Bill. Second, it is computed on the members present and voting, not on the entire strength of the two Houses, so those absent do not raise the threshold. Matches option A.

subject: History
stem: The Rowlatt Act was passed to _____________.
optB: Curtail the nationalist and revolutionary activities
optC: Have a favourable balance of trade
optD: Put second World War criminals on trial
solution: The Rowlatt Act of 1919, formally the Anarchical and Revolutionary Crimes Act, followed the report of the Sedition Committee headed by Justice Rowlatt. It let the government arrest without warrant, detain a suspect without trial and try political offences in camera without appeal, in effect carrying the emergency powers of the war years into peacetime. Its object was to suppress nationalist and revolutionary activity, which is why it was attacked as leaving no lawyer, no plea and no appeal, and why it provoked the Rowlatt Satyagraha and the events at Jallianwala Bagh. It concerned neither agrarian reform, nor the balance of trade, nor war-crimes trials, which in any case belong to a later war. Matches option B.

subject: Polity
chapter: Indian Constitution — Making, Foundation and Amendments
subtopic: Features, Parts and Schedules of Constitution
stem: Which one among the following features of the Constitution of India is indicative of the fact that real executive power is vested in the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister?
solution: The Constitution vests the executive power of the Union formally in the President under Article 53, but Article 74 requires the President to act on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister, and Article 75(3) makes that Council collectively responsible to the House of the People. Such a nominal head, bound by the advice of a Cabinet that must retain the confidence of the legislature, is precisely the parliamentary form of government. Of the other features named, federalism describes how power is divided between the Union and the States, a representative legislature describes how members reach the House, and universal adult franchise describes who is entitled to vote; none of the three says where real executive power rests. Matches option D.

subject: Polity
chapter: Government Structure — Parliament, Judiciary and Constitutional Bodies
stem:
In which among the following cases, the joint session of both the Houses of Parliament can be summoned?
1. To amend the Constitution.
2. When Bill has been pending with one House for more than six months after it was passed by the other.
3. When both the Houses disagree on the amendments to be made in a Bill.
4. When a Bill is passed by one House and is rejected by the other.
Codes:
solution: Article 108 allows the President to summon a joint sitting of the two Houses in three situations: the other House has rejected the Bill; the two Houses have finally disagreed on the amendments to be made in it; or more than six months have elapsed since the Bill was received by the other House without being passed. Those are statements 2, 3 and 4, and all three qualify. Any Bill to amend the Constitution is outside this provision entirely, because Article 368 requires such a Bill to be passed separately by each House by the prescribed special majority and provides no deadlock-breaking device, so statement 1 fails. Money Bills are excluded for the same structural reason, since the Council of States cannot reject them. Matches option B.
reviewNote: Rule 1: the four numbered cases are flattened onto one line with the 'Codes:' tail. Key B (2, 3 and 4) is correct - a joint sitting is not available for a Constitution amendment bill.

subject: Economics
subtopic: Five Year Plans and Indian Planning
stem: The Bombay Plan drafted by GD Birla and JRD Tata emphasised on ________.
optA: That the economy should be left to the dynamic investments by the private sector in heavy industries.
optB: The public sector investments in infrastructure and heavy industries.
optD: That the private sector should foot the bill of intensive and low return investments in the heavy industries.
solution: The Bombay Plan of 1944 was drawn up by leading industrialists including Jehangir Ratanji Dadabhoy Tata and Ghanshyam Das Birla. Its striking feature was that businessmen themselves argued for a large economic role for the State: the base of the economy, meaning infrastructure such as power, transport and irrigation, together with heavy and basic industries, was to be built by public investment, while private enterprise concentrated on consumer goods. The reason they gave was that these projects needed enormous outlays, took years to mature and yielded little in the short run, so private capital would not undertake them. That is the opposite of leaving heavy industry to the dynamism of private investors, and the opposite of asking the private sector to bear those low-return investments. The plan also worked to a fifteen-year horizon rather than an annual one. Matches option B.

subject: History
stem:
Consider the following statements
1. The Buddhists in Deccan excavated rock- cut Chaityas and the Vaishnavas, Shaivas and Jainas imitated these in later centuries.
2. The Vaishnavas, Shaivas and Jainas excavated temples at sites for distant from rock-cut chaityas.
Which of the statement(s) given is/are correct?
solution: The Buddhists began the rock-cut tradition of the Deccan, cutting chaitya halls and viharas into the basalt escarpments from about the second century BCE at Bhaja, Karle, Bedsa and Kanheri. In later centuries Vaishnava, Shaiva and Jaina patrons took up the same technique and repeated the same excavated forms, so the first statement holds. The second does not. Those later shrines were cut into the very same hills, and often at the same site: Ellora is the clearest instance, where Buddhist, Hindu and Jaina caves stand side by side in a single cliff, and Badami, Aihole and Elephanta lie within the same rock-cut belt. Sites were chosen for rock that would take an excavation, so the later groups worked close to the older chaityas, not far from them. Matches option A.
reviewNote: Rule 1: the two numbered statements are flattened onto one line. Key A is correct - statement 2 is false because the Vaishnava/Shaiva/Jaina excavations are at the SAME sites, not distant from the rock-cut chaityas.

subject: History
subtopic: Freedom Movement — INC, Gandhi and Independence
stem:
Consider the following statements.
1. The Champaran Satyagraha marked Gandhiji’s second appearance in Indian politics as a leader of the masses.
2. The Champaran Satyagraha was launched to address the problems faced by Indigo plantation workers.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
solution: Champaran in 1917 was Gandhiji's first Satyagraha on Indian soil and his first appearance here as a leader of the masses. He had returned from South Africa only in 1915 and, on Gokhale's advice, spent his first year travelling and observing rather than leading, so describing Champaran as his second such appearance is wrong. The second statement is sound. The cultivators of Champaran were bound by the tinkathia system to plant indigo on three-twentieths of their holding for the European planters, and when the synthetic dye destroyed the market the planters extracted compensation in cash. Gandhiji went there at the request of Rajkumar Shukla, and the enquiry that followed produced the Champaran Agrarian Act of 1918. Matches option B.
reviewNote: Rule 1: the two numbered statements are flattened onto one line. Key B is correct - Champaran was Gandhi's FIRST mass campaign in India, so statement 1 ('second appearance') is false.

subject: History
stem:
Consider the following statements
1. Charles Wood’s Despatch of 1854 laid exclusive emphasis on the development of higher education in India and neglected primary and secondary education.
2. The Carlyle Circular issued by FIW Carlyle sought to check the Spread of revolutionary activities in educational institutions.
Select the correct answer using the codes given below
solution: Consider the two statements separately. Wood's Despatch of 1854 is remembered precisely because it rejected the downward filtration idea, which had concentrated effort on higher education for a small class in the hope that learning would seep downward. In its place the Despatch laid out a complete graded system: vernacular primary schools at the base, Anglo-vernacular high schools and affiliated colleges above them, and universities at Calcutta, Bombay and Madras at the top, supported by grants in aid, teacher training institutions and provision for the education of women. Far from neglecting primary and secondary education it made their spread a declared responsibility of the state, so the first statement is false. The Carlyle Circular was issued in 1905 by the Chief Secretary to the Government of Bengal during the agitation against the partition of Bengal. It directed that students taking part in political meetings or in the boycott movement would forfeit scholarships, and that their schools and colleges would lose grants and even recognition. Its object was exactly to keep political and revolutionary activity out of educational institutions, so the second statement is true. Only the second holds. Matches option B.
reviewNote: [RESOLVED — a second, independent blind derivation reached the printed key (B) without seeing it or the earlier objection, so the key stands. Basis: Statement 1 is FALSE and is the reverse of the truth: Wood's Despatch of 1854 abandoned the downward filtration theory and laid down a graded system from vernacular primary schools up to universities, making mass education a state responsibility. Statement 2 is TRUE: the Carlyle Circular of 1905 threatened students and institutions taking part in political agitation with loss of scholarships, grants and recognition, in order to keep revolutionary activity out of educational institutions. The name in the stem is printed as FIW Carlyle; it is R.W. Carlyle, then Chief Secretary to the Government of Bengal.]

subject: History
subtopic: Freedom Movement — INC, Gandhi and Independence
stem:
Consider the following statements about Gandhiji’s thinking on the environment.
1. His environmental thinking is rooted in his larger philosophical and moral thinking.
2. He preferred sustainable environmental practices to nourish the soil and the natural world.
3. He laid emphasis on the rigorous ethic of non-injury in our treatment of animals.
Which of the statement(s) given above is/are correct?
solution: Gandhiji never treated the environment as a subject apart. His concern for it grew from the same moral position as the rest of his thought, that human wants must be limited because the earth has enough for everyone's need but not for everyone's greed, which establishes the first statement. He argued for practices that renew rather than exhaust the soil, favouring organic manure and village-scale production over chemical fertiliser and large-scale industry, which establishes the second. Ahimsa in his hands reached beyond human beings, and he held that a nation is to be judged by the way it treats its animals, which establishes the third. All three describe his position. Matches option C.
reviewNote: Rule 1: the three numbered statements are flattened onto one line.

subject: History
subtopic: European Trading and Early British Conquest
stem: Which one among the following is common to the Treaty of Yandaboo (1826), the Treaty of Salbai (1782) and the Treaty of Gandamak (1879)?
optA: With these treaties, various Indian powers formed alliances to defeat the British
optB: These treaties enabled the British to control the South Asian powers
optC: These treaties expedited the spread of Indian culture abroad
optD: These treaties gave an essential boost to enhanced trade in South Asia
solution: Take the three treaties in turn. Salbai in 1782 closed the First Anglo-Maratha War and secured the British twenty years of peace with the Marathas along with recognition of their position. Yandaboo in 1826 closed the First Anglo-Burmese War and transferred Assam, Manipur, Arakan and Tenasserim to the British, with a large indemnity. Gandamak in 1879, imposed during the Second Anglo-Afghan War, placed Afghan foreign relations under British direction and ceded frontier districts. In every case the British were the dictating or the gaining party, and what each treaty produced was an extension of British control over a power of the region. They were therefore not alliances of Indian powers formed to defeat the British, and their subject matter was territory and political control rather than cultural exchange or the promotion of trade. Matches option B.
reviewNote: TEXT DEFECT: the running header 'SAMPLE QUESTION PAPER-i' has bled onto the end of option (B). Trim before publishing. Key B is correct.

subject: History
subtopic: Freedom Movement — INC, Gandhi and Independence
stem: Which one among the following was the major demand of the Bardoli Satyagraha (1928) organised under the leadership of Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel?
optB: Increase in the rates of labour wage
optC: Rollback of newly enhanced revenue rate.
optD: Supply of agricultural inputs to the farmers at subsidised rate
solution: The Bombay government's revision settlement raised the land revenue assessment of Bardoli taluka in Surat district by about twenty-two per cent, and it did so when the cultivators had already suffered crop failure. Under Vallabhbhai Patel the peasants refused to pay and pressed a single demand, that the enhancement be withdrawn and the assessment enquired into. The enquiry that followed cut the increase to a little over six per cent and ordered the return of confiscated land. The movement was thus about the rate of revenue, not about ownership of land, not about wages, and not about subsidised inputs. It was during this struggle that the women of Bardoli gave Patel the title Sardar. Matches option C.

subject: History
stem: Which one among the following statements is not correct?
optA: Gandhara School of Art owed its origin to the Indo-Greek rulers but the real patrons of the school were the Kushans, especially Kanishka.
optB: Rich carving, elaborate ornamentations and complex symbolism were not the main features of the Gandhara sculpture.
optC: The Graeco-Roman architectural impact modified the structure of Buddhist Stupas.
optD: The artists of the Amravati School of Arts mainly used white marble.
solution: The question asks which statement is untrue. Gandhara sculpture is in fact characterised by rich carving, elaborate ornamentation and complex symbolism, worked mainly in grey schist under Greco-Roman influence, with wavy hair, folded drapery and modelled anatomy. The statement that denies these were its main features therefore asserts the opposite of the truth and is the incorrect one. The other three stand. The school did begin under the Indo-Greek rulers and found its real patrons in the Kushans, above all Kanishka. Greco-Roman architectural forms did modify the plan and the decoration of Buddhist stupas, adding niches, pillars and figured panels. And the Amaravati school of the lower Krishna valley did work chiefly in white marble, in contrast with the red sandstone of Mathura. Matches option B.

subject: Economics
subtopic: Five Year Plans and Indian Planning
stem: Which one among the following statements regarding the Eighth Five Year Plan in India is not correct?
optA: The plan was postponed by two years because of the political upheavals at the centre.
optB: It aimed at the high growth of both agriculture and manufacturing sectors.
optC: Its emphasis was on growth in export and import, improvement in the trade and current account deficit.
optD: It set before itself two principal objectives of growth with stability’ and growth with justice.
solution: The question asks which statement is untrue of the Eighth Plan, which ran from 1992 to 1997. Three of the four are accurate. It was indeed postponed by two years: it should have begun in 1990, but political instability at the Centre and the payments crisis pushed it to 1992, the intervening years being covered by annual plans. It did aim at high growth in agriculture and allied activities and in the manufacturing sector. And because it was the first plan framed after the reforms of 1991, growth of exports and imports and the correction of the trade and current account deficits were explicit concerns. The remaining statement misattributes a pair of slogans: growth with stability, coupled with the progressive achievement of self-reliance, was the declared objective of the Fourth Plan of 1969 to 1974, while growth with social justice and equality belongs to the Ninth Plan of 1997 to 2002. Matches option D.

subject: Economics
stem:
Which among the following statements is/are true with regard to WTO membership?
1. All WTO members automatically receive the most favourable nation status.
2. The 12th ministerial conference of the World Trade Organisation took place in Geneva.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
solution: Take the statements one at a time. Most favoured nation treatment is the first principle written into the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, and it binds every member of the World Trade Organisation: any advantage, favour or privilege granted by one member to the products of another must at once be extended unconditionally to the like products of all other members. It is not something a country has to negotiate separately, it follows from membership itself, so the first statement is correct. The twelfth Ministerial Conference of the organisation, having been postponed twice because of the pandemic, met in June 2022 at the organisation's own headquarters in Geneva and produced the package of decisions on fisheries subsidies, on the waiver relating to vaccine patents and on the moratorium on customs duties for electronic transmissions. The second statement is correct as well. Matches option C.
reviewNote: [KEY CORRECTED B -> C. Two independent derivations, each made without sight of the printed key, agree against it. This is publisher practice material rather than a past paper, so there is no issued key to preserve. The book prints B. Basis: Statement 1 is TRUE: most favoured nation treatment is the opening principle of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade and binds every member automatically, so a concession given to one must be extended to all. Statement 2 is TRUE: the twelfth Ministerial Conference was held in June 2022 at the organisation's headquarters in Geneva. Both hold.]

subject: Economics
stem: TRIPS (Trade Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights) agreement is administered by:
solution: TRIPS is one of the agreements annexed to the Marrakesh Agreement that established the World Trade Organization in 1995. Every member of that organisation is bound by it as part of the single undertaking; compliance is monitored by the Council for TRIPS and enforced through the organisation's dispute settlement machinery, which is what distinguishes it from earlier intellectual property treaties that carried no such enforcement. The United Nations Conference on Trade and Development works on trade and development policy but administers no binding agreement of this kind, the United Nations itself is not a party to it, and the World Bank is a lending institution. Note also that the older Paris and Berne Conventions, which TRIPS incorporates by reference, are administered by the World Intellectual Property Organization, but TRIPS itself is not. Matches option C.

subject: Current Affairs
stem:
Consider the following statements:
1. G-20 address issues related to the international financial stability, sustainable development and climate change mitigation.
2. India will host the G-20 summit in 2023.
3. The G20 was founded in response to several world economic crises.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
solution: All three statements hold. The agenda of the G20 began with international financial stability and has since widened to cover sustainable development and the mitigation of climate change, so the first is correct. India held the presidency of the grouping from December 2022 and hosted the leaders' summit at New Delhi in September 2023, so the second is correct. The grouping was itself created in 1999 as a forum of finance ministers and central bank governors in the aftermath of the Asian financial crisis and the other emerging-market crises of that decade, and was raised to the level of heads of state and government in 2008 during the global financial crisis, so the third is correct as well. Matches option A.
reviewNote: Rule 1: the three numbered statements are flattened onto one line. Key A (1, 2 and 3) is correct.

subject: Current Affairs
stem: India by becoming a full-fledged member of the Financial Action Task Force:
optA: Will be able to access information on suspect accounts in nations such as Switzerland and UK.
optB: Will play an important role in law enforcement matters, investigations or prosecutions of terrorist activities at an international level.
optC: Has also become a member of Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development.
solution: The Financial Action Task Force sets international standards against money laundering and terrorist financing; membership brings a country into its information-sharing arrangements, which is what gives access to details of suspect accounts held abroad. The task force is a standard-setting body and expressly not an investigating or prosecuting agency, so the enforcement claim overstates its role. It is also not the OECD - its secretariat is merely housed at OECD premises in Paris - so India does not gain OECD membership through it, and that in turn rules out the all-of-these option. Matches option A.
reviewNote: [RESOLVED — a second, independent blind derivation reached the printed key (A) without seeing it or the earlier objection, so the key stands. Basis: India became the thirty-fourth full member of the Financial Action Task Force in June 2010. The task force's own standards require members to cooperate and exchange information on suspect accounts, and Switzerland and the United Kingdom are members, so the first claim holds. The third is plainly false: the task force merely has its secretariat housed at the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development, and India is not a member of that body, which also disposes of the 'all of these' option. The second fails on a hard distinction, namely that the task force is a policy-making and standard-setting body and expressly not an investigating or prosecuting agency, so membership cannot confer a role in investigations or prosecutions. Confidence is medium rather than high because the second claim is loosely enough worded that a setter might have read it as describing India's wider role in the counter-terrorist-financing effort.]

subject: History
subtopic: Freedom Movement — INC, Gandhi and Independence
stem: Consider the following declaration and identify the person who made it using the codes given below? The time has come when badges of honour make our shame glaring in their incongruous context of humiliation and I, for my part, wish to stand shorn of all special distinction, by the side of my countrymen who, for their so-called insignificance are liable to suffer degradation not fit for human beings.
solution: These are the words of Rabindranath Tagore in his letter of 31 May 1919 to the Viceroy, Lord Chelmsford, renouncing the knighthood conferred on him in 1915. He wrote in the weeks after the massacre at Jallianwala Bagh on 13 April 1919, and the badges of honour he wished to be shorn of were the imperial titles that set him apart from countrymen being degraded. The identifying detail is the special distinction itself: only a titled man could ask to stand shorn of it. Gandhiji returned his Kaiser-i-Hind medal only in 1920 and in quite different words, Nehru held no such title, and Dadabhai Naoroji had died in 1917. Matches option D.

subject: History
subtopic: Freedom Movement — INC, Gandhi and Independence
stem: Identify, using the code given below, the nationalist leader who was sentenced’ in the words outlined below: ‘The fact that in the eyes of millions of your countrymen you are a great patriot and great leader’ but ’as a man subject to the law, who has, by his own admission broken the law ’you are subject to six years imprisonment Code:
solution: This is the sentence pronounced by the District and Sessions Judge, Broomfield, at Ahmedabad on 18 March 1922, in what came to be called the Great Trial, where the charge was sedition arising from articles in Young India. The accused had pleaded guilty and invited the severest penalty the law allowed, and the judge, while acknowledging that in the eyes of millions he was a great patriot and a great leader, held that a man subject to the law who admits breaking it must be punished, and awarded six years of simple imprisonment. The sentence of six years in 1922 is the identifying detail and belongs to this trial and this accused. Matches option B.

subject: History
subtopic: Freedom Movement — INC, Gandhi and Independence
stem: Consider the following statement: “We believe that it is the inalienable right of the Indian people as of any other people, to have freedom and to enjoy the fruits of their toil and have the necessities of life so that they may have full opportunities of growth.” Identify the correct context of this statement from below.
optA: Pledge of independence to be publicly taken all over India on 26 January, 1930.
optB: Preamble of the Constitution of India adopted in 1950.
optC: Congress Working Committee Resolution adopted at the special Calcutta Congress Session in 1920.
optD: Part of speech delivered by Subhash Chandra Bose at the launch of ‘Azad Hind Fauj’.
solution: These are the opening words of the declaration of independence drafted for the Congress and read out at public meetings across the country on 26 January 1930, when the pledge of Purna Swaraj was taken, following the Lahore session of December 1929 which had adopted complete independence as the goal. The declaration went on to say that a government which deprives a people of these rights may be altered or abolished. The wording is not from the Preamble, which speaks in the name of we the people of India and promises justice, liberty, equality and fraternity; the special Calcutta session of 1920 adopted the programme of non-cooperation rather than a statement of independence; and the Azad Hind Fauj was launched more than a decade after these words were written. Matches option A.

subject: Economics
stem: Which one among the following led to the Greece economic crisis 2010?
optD: Outflow of foreign capital due to political unrest
solution: Once Greece adopted the euro it could borrow at interest rates close to Germany's, and successive governments used that cheap credit to spend far beyond what they collected, on public sector employment, wages and pensions, while tax collection and evasion remained unaddressed. The true size of the deficit had also been understated in the figures reported to the European Union, and when the revised numbers were announced at the end of 2009 lenders lost confidence, bond yields rose and the country could no longer refinance its maturing debt. The cause was therefore unrestrained spending financed by easy loans. The rescue lending from the International Monetary Fund and the European partners came in 2010 as a response to the crisis, not a cause of it; the euro weakened after the crisis broke rather than before; and the trouble was fiscal, not a flight of foreign capital driven by political unrest. Matches option C.

subject: Current Affairs
stem: The Clean Development Mechanism (CDM), a mechanism to reduce greenhouse gas emission as per Kyoto Protocol implies that
optA: Industrial countries receive carbon credits by funding carbon saving projects in another relatively affluent nation.
optB: Industrial countries reduce their carbon emission by using environment friendly technology in production.
optC: Developed countries invest in carbon reduction in developing countries and receive carbon credit in return.
optD: Developed nations purchase carbon credit from other nations.
solution: The Kyoto Protocol imposed binding emission limits on the developed countries listed in Annex I and gave them three flexible mechanisms for meeting those limits at lower cost. Under the Clean Development Mechanism a developed country finances an emission-reducing project in a developing country that carries no binding limit, and earns Certified Emission Reductions equal to the saving, which it may count against its own target; the host country gains the investment and the cleaner technology. This is the one mechanism that links a developed with a developing country. Where one developed country undertakes such a project in another and both carry targets, the mechanism is Joint Implementation instead, so the description mentioning another relatively affluent nation belongs to that mechanism instead. Cutting one's own emissions at home requires no mechanism at all, and the outright purchase of credits is emissions trading. Matches option C.

solution: Consider the two proposed changes separately. Under the mechanism as it stood, the regulator fixed a floor price below which a certificate could not be sold and a forbearance price above which it could not, and trades took place within that band. The redesign put forward in 2021 removed both, leaving the price to be discovered by the market alone, so the statement that floor and forbearance prices are required to be specified describes the opposite of what was proposed and is incorrect. The same set of amendments widened the range of parties who could earn certificates. Generators who were receiving a subsidy or a concession, or a waiver of transmission or wheeling charges, had previously been shut out on the ground that they were already being supported; under the amendments they too were to be issued certificates. That statement is correct, so only the second of the two holds. Matches option B.

Statement I : A myopic person is advised to use concave lens.
Statement II : The eye lens of a myopic person focuses the parallel rays coming from front of the retina.
optA: Both the statements are individually true and statement II is the correct explanation of statement I.
optB: Both the statements are individually true but statement II is not the correct explanation of statement I.
optC: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
optD: Statement I is false but statement II is true.
solution: A short-sighted or myopic eye sees near objects clearly but not distant ones, because either the eyeball is too long from front to back or the eye lens converges too strongly. The result is that parallel rays arriving from a distant object are brought to a focus at a point in front of the retina, and by the time they reach the retina itself they have crossed and spread again, so the image formed there is blurred. The correction must therefore push the focus backward onto the retina. A concave lens is a diverging lens, so placing one before the eye makes the rays entering the eye slightly divergent instead of parallel; the eye's own lens then converges them a little further back than before and the focus falls exactly on the retina. The fact that the image forms short of the retina is thus precisely the reason a concave lens is prescribed, so the second statement explains the first. Matches option A.
reviewNote: [RESOLVED — a second, independent blind derivation reached the printed key (A) without seeing it or the earlier objection, so the key stands. Basis: Both statements are true and the second is the reason for the first. A myopic eye brings parallel rays from a distant object to a focus in FRONT of the retina, and the remedy is a diverging, that is concave, lens which makes the rays entering the eye spread so that the eye's own lens focuses them further back, on the retina. Statement II as printed reads 'coming from front of the retina', which is clumsy but recoverable, the sense being that the rays are focused in front of the retina; the wording should be tidied to 'in front of the retina'.]

Statement I : Oxidation in our body cells releases dangerous free radicals
Statement II : Our body itself produces antioxidants to neutralise harmful free radicals
optA: Both the statements are individually true and statement II is the correct explanation of statement I.
optB: Both the statements are individually true but statement II is not the correct explanation of statement I.
optC: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
optD: Statement I is false but statement II is true.
solution: The oxidation of nutrients in the mitochondria is not perfectly efficient. A small fraction of the oxygen used escapes the electron transport chain incompletely reduced, appearing as superoxide and other reactive species which carry an unpaired electron; these are free radicals, and they can damage cell membranes, proteins and deoxyribonucleic acid. The first statement is therefore true. The body does also make its own defences against them, among them the enzymes superoxide dismutase, catalase and glutathione peroxidase, besides the antioxidants it obtains from food, so the second statement is true as well. But the second describes how the damage is kept in check after the radicals have appeared; it says nothing about why oxidation should produce them in the first place, and a defence against a thing cannot be the cause of that thing. Both statements stand, and the second is not the explanation of the first. Matches option B.

Basis: Both statements are true but the second is not the explanation of the first: it describes how the body CONTAINS free radicals, not why oxidation generates them. A defence against something cannot be the cause of it.]

stem:
Statement I : Decay and disintegration of rock in situ is called weathering.
Statement II : Mechanical weathering is mainly caused by temperature variation.
optA: Both the statements are individually true and statement II is the correct explanation of statement I.
optB: Both the statements are individually true but statement II is not the correct explanation of statement I.
optC: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
optD: Statement I is false but statement II is true.
solution: Judge each statement on its own first, then ask whether the second accounts for the first. The first statement is true. Weathering is defined as the breakdown, decay and disintegration of rock where it lies, and the phrase 'in situ' is the essential part of the definition: the debris is loosened but not carried away. Once the loosened material is transported by running water, ice, wind or waves, the process being described is erosion, not weathering. The second statement is true as well. Mechanical, or physical, weathering breaks rock into smaller fragments without altering its chemical composition, and its principal agent is change of temperature. Rock is a poor conductor, so on heating the outer skin expands more than the interior and on cooling it contracts more, and the repeated stress makes the surface layers peel away or the rock split along its joints. Water freezing in cracks does the same work, since ice occupies more space than the water it came from and prises the rock apart. So both statements are individually true. The second, however, is not the explanation of the first. The first is a definition, and it covers every kind of weathering, chemical and biological as well as mechanical. The second picks out one class only, the mechanical class, and names an agent that produces it. Naming a cause of one sub-type does not explain why breakdown in place is what the term weathering means, nor why transport is excluded from it. Both statements are individually true, but the second is not the correct explanation of the first. Matches option B.
reviewNote: [KEY CORRECTED C -> B. A third derivation, made without sight of the key or of the earlier attempts, independently reached the same answer as an earlier blind pass. Two independent derivations against the printed key. This is publisher practice material, not a past paper, so there is no issued key to preserve; the book prints C. Basis: Both statements are individually true. Weathering is by definition the decay and disintegration of rock in place, with no transport of the debris; once the loosened material is carried away the process is erosion. Mechanical weathering, which breaks rock apart without changing its chemical composition, is chiefly driven by temperature change, through differential expansion and contraction of the outer layers and through the freezing of water in joints. But the second does not explain the first. The first statement is a definition of weathering as a whole, covering chemical and biological weathering as well; the second names a cause of only one class of it and says nothing about why in-place breakdown is what the word denotes or why transport is excluded. Naming a cause of one sub-type cannot account for a general definition. Marked medium because a reader who treats 'gives a mechanism for' as sufficient for 'explains' would reach the other verdict; on the usual convention, where the second statement must give the reason the first is true, it does not.]

Statement I : The semi-arid tracts of India stretching from eastern Rajasthan in the north to south central Tamil Nadu are agriculturally less productive.
Statement II : The semi-arid tracts are homeland to a large number of central Indian Scheduled Tribe population
optA: Both the statements are individually true and statement II is the correct explanation of statement I.
optB: Both the statements are individually true but statement II is not the correct explanation of statement I.
optC: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
optD: Statement I is false but statement II is true.
solution: The semi-arid belt that runs from eastern Rajasthan through Madhya Pradesh and the interior of the Deccan down to south-central Tamil Nadu receives rainfall that is both scanty and highly variable from year to year, its soils are thin and its irrigation largely unassured. Farming there is chiefly rainfed and given over to coarse millets and pulses, and yields are among the lowest and least dependable in the country, so the first statement is true. The same tract takes in the Bhil country of southern Rajasthan and western Madhya Pradesh and the Gond and Korku areas of the Satpura hills and Vidarbha, so a large part of the tribal population of central India does indeed live within it, and the second statement is true as well. The two are not related as effect and cause. The poor productivity of the tract follows from the shortage and unreliability of its rainfall and the poverty of its soils; the presence of a tribal population explains nothing about the yields, and the causal arrow if any runs the other way, the difficulty of the country being part of why such populations have remained there. Both statements are true and the second is not the explanation of the first. Matches option B.
reviewNote: [RESOLVED — a second, independent blind derivation reached the printed key (B) without seeing it or the earlier objection, so the key stands. Basis: Both statements are broadly true, but the second cannot explain the first: low productivity follows from scanty and unreliable rainfall and thin soils, not from who lives in the tract. Statement II is defensible because the belt takes in the Bhil country of southern Rajasthan and western Madhya Pradesh and the Gond areas of the Satpura and Vidarbha region. Confidence is medium only because that overlap is a matter of degree; the verdict is unaffected either way in one direction, since if statement II were judged false the answer would instead be the 'first true, second false' option.]

subject: Geography
stem:
Statement I : The Mediterranean climate is hig- hly suitable for fruit production.
Statement II : Cool and moist winters in Mediter- ranean regions enable ample production of fruits.
optA: Both the statements are individually true and statement II is the correct explanation of statement I.
optB: Both the statements are individually true but statement II is not the correct explanation of statement I.
optC: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
optD: Statement I is false but statement II is true.
solution: Consider the two statements against what the Mediterranean type of climate actually is. Its defining feature is a reversal of the usual pattern: the summers are hot, dry and cloudless, while the rain comes in the mild winter half of the year. The first statement is true. These lands are the orchard lands of the world, famous for citrus fruits, grapes, olives and figs, and fruit growing is their characteristic form of agriculture. The second statement is true as a description of the climate, and it also states the reason the first is true. Since the summer is virtually rainless, the trees receive practically their entire supply of moisture during the cool wet winter; they survive the summer drought because they are deep-rooted and draw on the water stored below, and because thick bark and small waxy leaves check evaporation, but the water they draw on is the winter rain. The mildness of those winters matters just as much, because citrus is destroyed by frost and can only be grown where the cold season stays gentle. So the winter rain sustains the trees while the long sunny summer ripens the fruit, and it is the cool moist winter that makes such orchard farming possible in the first place. Both statements are true and the second is the correct explanation of the first. Matches option A.
reviewNote: [KEY CORRECTED C -> A. A third derivation, made without sight of the key or of the earlier attempts, independently reached the same answer as an earlier blind pass. Two independent derivations against the printed key. This is publisher practice material, not a past paper, so there is no issued key to preserve; the book prints C. Basis: Both statements are true and the second gives the reason for the first. The Mediterranean type of climate has hot, dry, sunny summers and mild, moist winters, with almost all the rain falling in the cooler half of the year, and these lands are the classic orchard lands, growing citrus, grapes, olives and figs, so the first statement is true. The second is true as a description and is also causal: the trees receive effectively their whole moisture supply from the winter rains, since the summer is rainless, and the mildness of the winter keeps the groves free of the frost that would destroy citrus. So the character of the winters is what makes the fruit growing possible. Marked medium because one could argue the hot dry sunny summer, which ripens the fruit, is an equally necessary half of the reason and that the second statement is therefore incomplete rather than explanatory; but an incomplete reason that is nonetheless the operative one is normally accepted as the correct explanation, and winter moisture is the limiting factor here.]

subject: Geography
stem:
Statement I : In the Northern hemisphere, the ocean currents flowing from equator towards the North pole and from pole towards the equator are deflected to their right.
Statement II : This happens due to rotation of the Earth on the axis from West to East Reasons of Ocean Currents Ocean Currents
optA: Both the statements are individually true and statement II is the correct explanation of statement I.
optB: Both the statements are individually true but statement II is not the correct explanation of statement I.
optC: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
optD: Statement I is false but statement II is true.
solution: Anything that moves freely over the surface of the rotating Earth is turned aside from a straight path, to the right of its direction of travel in the northern hemisphere and to the left in the southern, and this holds whichever way the body happens to be heading. That is why the currents of the North Atlantic and the North Pacific form great clockwise gyres, the warm water moving poleward along the western side of the ocean and the cooler water returning towards the equator along the eastern side, each of them swinging to its own right. So the first statement is true. The deflection is the Coriolis effect, and it arises because the Earth spins on its axis from west to east while the surface itself travels eastward much faster near the equator than near the poles; water carrying the greater eastward speed of low latitudes into higher latitudes therefore runs ahead of the ground beneath it and appears to curve. The rotation of the Earth is thus the cause of the deflection, so the second statement explains the first. Matches option A.
reviewNote: [RESOLVED — a second, independent blind derivation reached the printed key (A) without seeing it or the earlier objection, so the key stands. Basis: Both statements are true and the second is the cause. Deflection to the right in the northern hemisphere, whatever the direction of travel, is the Coriolis effect, and the Coriolis effect arises from the Earth's rotation on its axis from west to east. Note that the stem carries trailing text, 'Reasons of Ocean Currents Ocean Currents', which is a page heading that has bled into the transcription and should be trimmed; it does not affect the answer.]
